clue.text: Rex might be found here, but suffering from lack of favor.

definitions.meaning: first meaning, taken literally: Rex is a stock name for a dog, and a dog lives in its kennel
second meaning: the idiom for being out of favour with someone

explanation.walkthrough: Rex reads like a king (Latin rex), but here it is the classic name for a pet dog, whose house is a kennel.
explanation.definitionFit: The idiom describes someone who has fallen out of a partner's or boss's good graces and is in disgrace.

clue.text: Opera that is a bit short of being ordinary?

indicators.note: a bit short of says the word falls one small piece short, so its last letter is dropped

parts.note: ordinary means normal

explanation.surface: A wry question whether some opera is just slightly less than ordinary.
explanation.definitionFit: Norma is Bellini's opera about a Druid priestess, so it is an example of the genre.

clue.text: It might represent a peak of learning, to employ audibly a point concerning Shylock's money with one on.

definitions.text: It might represent a peak of learning

indicators.note: audibly says the word for employing is to be taken by its sound, which matches a word meaning loftier

parts.note: to employ someone is to hire them
E (east) is a point of the compass
the ducat is the coin Shylock lends in The Merchant of Venice
I is the Roman numeral one
taken as written

explanation.surface: A rambling sentence that seems to tie scholarship to the moneylender of Shakespeare's Venice.
explanation.walkthrough: 'audibly' says HIRE (to employ) is heard as HIGHER; 'concerning' and 'with' only join the pieces, and 'on' is used as written at the end.
explanation.definitionFit: University study is the level above school, so it can stand for the summit of a person's schooling.

clue.text: The line possibly signed on by little Dorothy and little Theodore.

definitions.note: the definition describes the answer as an adjective for a line, the one you sign a contract on

parts.note: Dot is the pet form of the name Dorothy
Ted is the pet form of the name Theodore

explanation.surface: Two children called Dot and Ted put their names to an agreement.
explanation.walkthrough: The idiom 'sign on the dotted line' makes the definition fair: the answer describes the kind of line people sign on.
explanation.definitionFit: Forms mark the place for a signature with a row of dots, the familiar line of the contract idiom.

clue.text: With a shaggy rat, I only notice there's a lot of turning with it.

indicators.note: With signals that the answer is carried along with these words, lying across shaggy rat, I only

parts.note: the letters run on from the end of shaggy through rat and I into the start of only

explanation.surface: Someone holding a scruffy rat notices only that it keeps spinning round.
explanation.walkthrough: 'With' signals the answer travelling along with the words: it runs across the end of 'shaggy', all of 'rat' and 'I', and the start of 'only'.
explanation.definitionFit: Gyration is circular or spiral motion, which means plenty of whirling round.

clue.text: A common comparison with aging implied.

definitions.text: A common comparison with aging implied

parts.words: A common comparison with aging implied
parts.note: the clue describes a stock simile for great age, named after the oldest man in the Bible

explanation.definitionFit: Methuselah is said in Genesis to have lived 969 years, so likening someone to him is a familiar simile for extreme antiquity.

clue.text: Taken aback, and getting us up right before it ends up given leverage.

indicators.note: before places the right abbreviation ahead of the final piece
in a down entry, up means the word us is written from the bottom upwards

parts.note: a lid given leverage with a tool is prised open

explanation.surface: Someone startled while being hauled upright, then levered into place.
explanation.walkthrough: 'up' turns US into SU, and 'before' puts R ahead of PRISED; 'it ends up' only says that piece finishes the answer.
explanation.definitionFit: Being taken aback is the feeling of being startled by something unexpected, which is what the answer names.

clue.text: A group of quatrains, first class in a precious stone at the end.

indicators.note: the end puts this short word last of all, after the stone
in places the first-class letters inside the precious stone

parts.note: a ruby is a red precious stone
A1 means first class, written AI in crosswords
taken as written

explanation.surface: A poetry collection praised as top quality, set like a gem.
explanation.walkthrough: A1 (first class) is written AI, and 'in' puts it inside RUBY to make RUBAIY; 'the end' puts AT after it.
explanation.definitionFit: The Rubaiyat of Omar Khayyam is famous as a sequence of four-line stanzas in FitzGerald's translation.

clue.text: One hears it is passed on, having been given a new color.

definitions.text: having been given a new color

indicators.note: One hears says the word for passing on is to be taken by its sound, which matches a colouring word

parts.note: to pass on is to die, so something passed on has died

explanation.surface: A rumour is spread about something that has just been recoloured.
explanation.walkthrough: 'passed on' looks like handing something along, but it is the euphemism for dying; 'One hears' says DIED is heard as the colouring word.
explanation.definitionFit: Fabric soaked in a colouring agent takes on a fresh hue, which is the past participle of the colouring verb.

clue.text: Not a grand type, but rather moral.

definitions.meaning: first meaning: a piano with a vertical frame, the kind that is not a grand
second meaning: honest and decent in conduct

explanation.walkthrough: 'grand' looks like an ordinary adjective, but it is the grand piano, and the other common type of piano stands vertically.
explanation.definitionFit: The word means both a vertical piano and a person of strict integrity.

clue.text: Right, my dear? Wrong–but Muscovites in uniform might swell it.

definitions.text: Muscovites in uniform might swell it

indicators.note: Wrong says the letters are in the wrong order and must be rearranged

parts.note: taken as written

explanation.surface: Someone checks they are correct with a partner, then is told about uniformed Moscow men.
explanation.definitionFit: The Soviet land force was known by its revolutionary colour, so Russian soldiers joined and enlarged it.

clue.text: A cellar might be what puts you in the lowest category.

definitions.text: what puts you in the lowest category

parts.note: a cellar is a basement, the storey below ground

explanation.surface: An underground room is imagined as the bottom division of some ranking.
explanation.definitionFit: Abasement is humiliation, being brought low and treated as of the meanest rank.

clue.text: Quiet, radical–strip!

parts.note: sh is the call for quiet
a Red is a political radical

explanation.surface: A command to hush, then to a revolutionary to undress.
explanation.definitionFit: To strip something into ribbons is to tear it to pieces, the same as the answer as a verb.

clue.text: One of the damn people onstage, with any confusion leading to a cry of alarm coming back.

definitions.text: One of the damn people onstage

indicators.note: leading to puts the jumbled word first, ahead of the cry
confusion says the word any is jumbled

parts.note: taken as written

indicators.note: coming back means the squeal is written backwards

parts.note: eek is a squeal of alarm

explanation.surface: An actor in a cursed stage show, with a muddle ending in a shriek.
explanation.walkthrough: Damn Yankees is a 1955 Broadway musical about a baseball team. 'confusion' turns ANY into YAN, 'coming back' turns EEK into KEE, and 'leading to' puts YAN first.
explanation.definitionFit: The musical's title names the New York baseball team, and each player in it is one member of that team.

clue.text: The direction of neither's companion on the middle sat a bit awkwardly.

indicators.note: on puts the companion word in front of the rest

parts.note: nor goes with neither in 'neither ... nor'

indicators.note: a bit awkwardly says the words the and sat are mixed up

parts.note: taken as written
taken as written

explanation.surface: Someone sat clumsily in the middle, with directions given in an odd grammar.
explanation.walkthrough: 'a bit awkwardly' mixes THE and SAT into THEAST, and 'on' puts NOR in front; 'middle' gives no letters.
explanation.definitionFit: It is the compass point halfway between two cardinal points, so it is a direction.

clue.text: What one described by 1 across is asked to shake–worse in the inside, possibly, but capable of giving the best cuts.

definitions.text: capable of giving the best cuts

indicators.note: in the inside puts the rearranged letters within the dog's foot

parts.words: What one described by 1 across is asked to shake
parts.note: 1 across tells us we have a dog, and a dog is asked to shake a paw

indicators.note: possibly says the word worse is rearranged

parts.note: taken as written

explanation.surface: A pet told to shake hands, with something worse inside, ends up cutting well.
explanation.walkthrough: The dog of 1 across is asked to shake a PAW; 'possibly' rearranges WORSE into OWERS, and 'in the inside' puts it within the paw.
explanation.definitionFit: A motor-driven saw slices timber far more cleanly and quickly than a hand tool, hence the boast.

clue.text: Half of what goes all around the town in song. (A sort of stew on a dish type in addition–there's a story here!)

definitions.text: Half of what goes all around the town in song

indicators.note: on puts the jumbled word ahead of the dish
A sort of says the word stew is turned into another sort of word by jumbling

parts.note: taken as written
a side is a side dish

explanation.surface: A cookery note on stew and side dishes, with a nudge that a tale lies here.
explanation.walkthrough: The song is 'The Sidewalks of New York': 'East Side, West Side, all around the town'. 'A sort of' turns STEW into WEST, and 'on' puts it before SIDE; 'there's a story here!' points to West Side Story.
explanation.definitionFit: The song line names two halves of Manhattan, and this is the second of them.

clue.text: Small canine, with not too much bite.

definitions.text: Small canine, with not too much bite

parts.words: Small canine, with not too much bite
parts.note: the clue describes a young dog, whose nip is mild, with canine also hinting at the tooth

explanation.definitionFit: A puppy is a young dog, small and with a gentle, playful nip rather than a real bite.

clue.text: A high point out back to you and me, being all wound up in the worst way.

definitions.text: all wound up in the worst way

parts.note: a tor is a rocky hilltop

indicators.note: back says the word out is written in reverse

parts.note: taken as written
us is you and me

explanation.surface: A climber on a summit gets anxious about the way back home.
explanation.walkthrough: TOR is a rocky hill, common in place names on Dartmoor in south-west England; 'back' turns OUT into TUO.
explanation.definitionFit: The adjective means full of twists, so a route or argument coiled up to excess fits it.

clue.text: Dashes frantically from old ghosts.

indicators.note: frantically says the letters of dashes are rushed about into a new order

explanation.surface: Someone races in panic away from long-dead spirits.
explanation.definitionFit: Shades is the poetic word for spirits of the dead, as in the classical underworld.

clue.text: Question, in the way of the surrounding state.

indicators.note: surrounding says the style phrase goes around the questioning word

parts.note: a la (French) means in the style or way of
to question is to ask

explanation.surface: An enquiry about the manner of the region round about.
explanation.definitionFit: Alaska is the largest of the fifty American states.

clue.text: Stressed? No! But starts like Schwartz does.

indicators.note: starts like says only the opening part of the surname is used, its tail dropped

explanation.surface: Someone denies being tense, and points out how a surname begins.
explanation.definitionFit: A schwa is the neutral vowel heard in unstressed syllables, like the a in about.

clue.text: Proving a bad ruse could be positive.

indicators.note: bad says the word ruse is put into a bad, jumbled order

explanation.surface: A poor trick still turns out well.
explanation.definitionFit: Being certain of something is being sure, the same as feeling positive about it.

clue.text: Said incorrectly, and loses color around it, being a line of cliffs.

indicators.note: around puts the paling word outside the jumbled letters

parts.note: someone who loses colour pales

indicators.note: incorrectly says the letters of said are in the wrong order

explanation.surface: Someone misspeaks and goes white, standing by the cliffs.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Said' looks like the verb of the surface but is fodder: 'incorrectly' scrambles it to ISAD, and 'around' puts PALES outside it, with 'it' pointing back to that jumble.
explanation.definitionFit: The Palisades are the long row of steep cliffs on the Hudson, and the word names any such line.

clue.text: Possibly cored as a sort of ornamentation.

indicators.note: Possibly says the word cored could be rearranged into another word

explanation.surface: An apple with its centre removed could be a decorative touch.
explanation.definitionFit: Decor is the furnishing and decoration of a room, its adornment.

clue.text: Saw in the newspapers there's a way to pass on the contents of it, being so prepared.

indicators.note: the contents of it says the dying word goes inside the reading word, as its filling

parts.note: you read something you saw in the papers
to die is a way to pass on

explanation.surface: A reader spots in the press how an estate passes on, and is ready for it.
explanation.walkthrough: 'the contents of it' makes DIE the filling of READ: REA, then DIE, then D.
explanation.definitionFit: To ready something is to prepare it, so being so prepared is the past participle of that verb.

clue.text: A couple might run off to get it, as the film might be.

definitions.text: A couple might run off to get it
definitions.meaning: first meaning: married, the slang sense of the answer, as eloping lovers are
second meaning: joined end to end, as pieces of film are edited together

explanation.walkthrough: 'run off' is the eloping couple; 'get spliced' is slang for getting married.
explanation.definitionFit: The word means joined or married in slang, and also the joining of cut lengths of movie stock.

clue.text: Office types having the wrong notes on a chart, with some signs of hesitation.

indicators.note: on puts the jumbled notes before the chart
wrong says the letters of notes are in the wrong order

parts.note: taken as written
a graph is a chart
er is a sound of hesitation, so several are ers

explanation.surface: Clerks fumble their notes over a chart, umming and erring.
explanation.walkthrough: 'wrong' turns NOTES into STENO, and 'on' puts it before GRAPH; ERS are the ums and ers of hesitation.
explanation.definitionFit: These office workers take dictation in shorthand, a classic clerical job.
